prime.problem: Every brace, space and repeated key in an answer costs one forward pass of waiting. Pretty-printed JSON spends half its tokens on layout. If you don't know which tokens are expensive (the ones written, not the ones read), you'll shrink the prompt and wonder why nothing got faster.
prime.fits: Last card of part 6. It applies the output-length law from the llm-latency course to structured answers, and explains most of the course's "constrained was 2× faster" result: 38 tokens instead of 80.
expect: minified JSON, delimited formats, dropped fields
prime.goal: Estimate the time saved by a more compact output format on a given host, and decide when minified JSON is enough and when a custom format is worth losing JSON's tooling.

attend: Why did shrinking incident.io's input 7.5× save only 1.3 s, while shrinking its output 3.4× saved 3.4 s?
Pretty JSON is 72 tokens and minified 35 for the same data. Where did the other 37 go, and does the parser need any of them?
Why is the pipe format only guaranteed if you also write a grammar for it?
Why is replacing UUIDs with small ints helpful, but replacing city names with ints harmful?
On which host does a 54-token saving stop mattering, and why?

must: Output is written one token per forward pass, input is read in one parallel prefill → an output token cost roughly 280× an input token in the incident.io case → cut answer tokens first

Layout (spaces, newlines, indentation) and repeated key names are tokens the parser doesn't need → minified JSON 72 → 35, pipe format 18 → writing time falls in proportion (4.68 → 2.27 → 1.17 s at 15.4 tok/s)

A custom format loses JSON's ecosystem → no JSON Schema grammar, validator or engine support unless you write your own → minified JSON keeps most of the saving at zero risk; go delimited only for simple, flat answers
Saving = tokens saved ÷ output speed → the same 54 tokens are 3.5 s on the M3 but 0.03 s on a 1,745 tok/s host → the lever matters most on slow hosts and at high volume
elevated: Constrained decoding often emits no whitespace at all (38 tokens vs 80 unconstrained on the M3) → much of the "grammar made it faster" effect is this compaction, not faster tokens → you may already have the saving
reference: the exact token counts per format (72, 35, 18; YAML 42; UUID 35)

compress.prompt: From memory, write the time formula and, under it, rank these five by how much time they save for our order: minify, pipe format, drop a reasoning field, shrink the pasted schema, remap long IDs. One reason per rank.
checklist: output tokens dominate because they're written one per pass; input is read in parallel
minify removes layout only and keeps full JSON tooling
a delimited format removes key names and punctuation too, but loses JSON tooling
dropping a reasoning field is the biggest cut when there is one, but it removes information and can cost accuracy
shrinking the prompt (the 286-token schema) mostly saves prefill, which is small
ID remapping helps when IDs are long opaque strings, not when values carry meaning

retrieve.q: Explain why the output side of an answer is so much more expensive than the input side, using the card's formula.
answer: prefill reads all input tokens in one parallel pass
each output token needs its own forward pass
so the time is roughly prefill + n_out ÷ output speed, and n_out is the term you can shrink cheaply

retrieve.q: Walk through the incident.io rewrite step by step: what changed, how many tokens, and what each step saved.
answer: drop the reasoning field: output 315 → 170, 11 → 7 s
compact input: 15,000 → 2,000 tokens, 7 → 5.7 s, only 1.3 s
overall 11 → 2.3 s, 4.8× faster, mostly from output

retrieve.q: Your nested schema has optional fields and arrays of objects. Pipe format or minified JSON? Justify with the card's numbers and warnings.
answer: minified JSON: keeps most of the saving (72 → 35) and every schema, grammar and validator still works
pipe format would need your own grammar for nesting and optional fields, or you're back to parsing and repair
the cookbook warns an unfamiliar format can hurt quality on complex tasks

compare.q: The latency course's output-length card and this one use the same law. What does a structured answer add to it: which tokens are cheap to remove here that aren't in prose?
answer: same law: time grows linearly with output tokens
in JSON, layout and repeated keys carry no information the parser needs, so removing them costs nothing
in prose almost every token carries content; cutting length means saying less

compare.q: Compact formats remove tokens; fast-forward keeps them but stops sampling forced ones. Which works on which stack, and do they stack?
answer: compact output works everywhere, including hosted APIs
fast-forward only on engines that implement it (Guidance, SGLang's jump-forward)
they stack partly: a compact format has fewer forced key tokens left to skip

predict.q: Your constrained M3 runs already emit compact JSON (38 tokens). You switch to the pipe format (18 tokens) with a matching grammar. Predict the time saved per answer and per 10,000 answers at the constrained run's 17.47 tok/s, before computing. Then: would the same switch be worth it on a 66 tok/s hosted model?
predict.answer: About 1.1 s per answer: 20 fewer tokens ÷ 17.47 tok/s ≈ 1.14 s, or about 3.2 hours per 10,000 answers. On a 66 tok/s host the same 20 tokens are 0.3 s, under an hour per 10,000. Whether that's worth losing JSON's tooling depends on volume; the cookbook's warning about unfamiliar formats applies either way.

apply.task: Take one structured answer your own system produces. Write it three ways: pretty JSON, minified JSON, and a delimited line format. Count tokens for each with your model's tokenizer (Ollama: prompt_eval_count of the text minus an empty baseline, with raw: true). Compute writing time at your measured output speed, and the saving per 10,000 answers for minify and for delimited.
apply.done: You have three token counts, three writing times and two savings per 10,000, and a one-line decision: minify only, or delimited with a grammar, and why.
apply.hint: The card's reference for the order: 72 / 35 / 18 tokens; at 15.4 tok/s that's 4.68 / 2.27 / 1.17 s, and pretty → minified saves about 6.7 h per 10,000 answers. If your answer is nested, the delimited version will need escaping rules; count that as a cost.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the per-answer saving, or whether it matters on a fast host?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the input side saved so little at incident.io?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: output tokens → time, or format choice → lost tooling and quality?
Which fields in your own answers exist only for humans reading logs?
Looking back over the course: which lever (p, n, TPOT, GCT) would you pull first on your own workload?
